text: A REST or GraphQL API has no page layout and often no rendered HTML at all, so most of the main OWASP Top 10's web-focused language doesn't map cleanly onto a JSON request and response cycle. That's why OWASP maintains a separate API Security Top 10, currently the 2023 edition, built around authorization failures specific to how APIs expose objects and functions — and every technique here still assumes the same signed, authorized scope as the rest of this chapter.

Broken Object Level Authorization, BOLA, is API1:2023 and the most-cited API finding in real engagements. It happens when an API checks that you're authenticated but never checks that the specific object you're requesting actually belongs to you. The test is almost always the same shape: authenticate as User A, note an object's ID, then replay that exact request authenticated as User B. If User B can read or modify User A's order, that's BOLA, full stop.

Mass assignment happens when an endpoint blindly binds every field in a submitted body to a backend object instead of allow-listing specific fields. A profile-update request meant only to change a display name might also include role or accountBalance — fields the UI never exposed. If the backend naively applies the whole body, those fields get set anyway. GraphQL mutations need the exact same scrutiny, since an input type can expose far more settable fields than any client ever actually sends.

Missing or weak rate limiting isn't just a performance concern — OWASP tracks it as its own category, Unrestricted Resource Consumption, because its absence directly enables brute-forcing a password reset code, enumerating every valid user ID at scale against a BOLA-vulnerable endpoint, or running up real cost on a metered backend until the bill itself becomes the attack.

Testing it is straightforward: fire a realistic burst of requests at a sensitive endpoint like login, OTP verification, or password reset, and confirm the API actually throttles, locks out, or rejects after a defined threshold — not just that a 429 response exists somewhere in the documentation.

That closes out this chapter's web and API testing checklist — the OWASP Top 10, injection and cross-site scripting, authentication and session flaws, and now BOLA, mass assignment, and rate limiting on the API side. Next chapter moves past the web application entirely, into what happens after an authorized engagement gets its first real foothold on a system.
